section_titles: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
periods.activity_title: Parv's Birthday and the Mystery of 29 February

tasks_in_class.description: Notice the number of days in February in the years 2024 and 2025 using the printed calendar grids.
Fill in the blanks with consecutive leap years before and after 2024.
We know that most years have 365 days. How many days would a leap year have?
Answer questions by writing appropriate days of the week: today, yesterday, tomorrow, day after tomorrow, day before yesterday.

time_bands.activity: Open with Parv's story: a child whose birthday falls on 29 February. Ask students how often they think that birthday comes. Display the February 2024 and February 2025 calendar grids and invite students to count the days in each, leading into Let Us Do Q1, p.175 ("Notice the number of days in February in 2024 and 2025....")

Students examine the two February grids, state their counts, and explain why one year has 29 days. Guide the class to define a leap year. Move to Let Us Do Q2, p.176 ("Fill in the blanks with consecutive leap years....") and Let Us Do Q3, p.176 ("How many days would a leap year have?...") — students fill blanks and share reasoning aloud.

Shift attention to the days-of-the-week vocabulary. Students work on Let Us Do Q5, p.176 ("Answer questions by writing appropriate days: today, yesterday, tomorrow...."). Pairs compare answers; the class resolves any disagreements by anchoring to a chosen start-day on the calendar grid.

Quick class discussion: what pattern governs when a leap year falls? Students say the rule in their own words. Briefly name the remaining calendar tasks — the months, festival names, date format, and elapsed time — to frame what the calendar grid can do.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'every four years' with 'every four years counting from any year' — anchor the pattern by listing 2020, 2024, 2028 on the board and asking what the gap always is. The printed February grids are the primary model here; if the textbook grids are not visible to all, draw a quick 7-column grid on the board for 2024 and 2025. Let Us Do Q4 (p.176) is a personal festival-month task that works well as take-home reflection.

section_titles: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
periods.activity_title: Date Detectives: Format, Patterns and Elapsed Time

tasks_in_class.description: July 1 is a Monday. Write the dates for the next two Mondays.
Notice the day on which July 15 falls; find August 15, September 15, October 15. What pattern do you notice? Challenge friends to guess the same date in the following month.
Laali born 04/07/2014 and Chotu born 04/12/2019. Who is older and by how much? Find Laali's 5th birthday and Chotu's 10th birthday dates.
Check manufacturing and expiry dates on a biscuit packet wrapper. Find (a) how old the packet is and (b) how many more days it is safe to eat.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the DD/MM/YYYY date format using a real or drawn biscuit packet. Ask students to read out dates aloud. Move to Let Us Do Q6, p.176 ("July 1 is a Monday. Write the dates for the next two Mondays....") — students count forward in sevens on the July grid and record results.

Present Let Us Do Q9, p.177 ("Notice the day on which July 15 falls; find August 15, September 15, October 15...."). Students use the calendar grids to fill in the days, then discuss in pairs what shift they notice each time the month advances. Invite two or three students to state the pattern; the class tests it by guessing ahead one more month.

Students work on Let Us Do Q7, p.176 ("Laali born 04/07/2014 and Chotu born 04/12/2019. Who is older and by how much?....") and Let Us Do Q8, p.177 ("Check manufacturing and expiry dates on a biscuit packet wrapper...."). Encourage students to write out the calculation steps in full before stating the answer.

Whole-class share: one student explains Q7 reasoning (years first, then months), another explains Q8 (count from manufacture to today, then to expiry). Resolve any disagreements about direction of counting (older = earlier date).

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in elapsed-time tasks is subtracting months without considering which month comes first in the year — use the number-line idea on the months (January = 1, December = 12) to keep direction clear. The pattern in Q9 shifts by one or two days per month depending on month length; let students discover this rather than stating it upfront. Let Us Do Q4 (p.176) may be used as a take-home or quick warm-up personal reflection.
materials: A biscuit or packet wrapper showing manufacturing and expiry dates (or a drawn example on the board)

periods.activity_title: Calendars All Around: Community Time and Festival Months

tasks_in_class.description: Explore names of months in Hindu/Islamic/Sikh or community calendar. Find year-start, correspondence to English months, festival months, new/full moon patterns and their names.

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: does every community begin its year on 1 January? Invite students to name festivals they know and ask which month or season they fall in. Record responses on the board under the community name to prime the exploration.

Students work in small groups on Let Us Explore Q1–5, p.177 ("Explore names of months in Hindu/Islamic/Sikh or community calendar. Find year-start, correspondence to English months, festival months, new/full moon patterns...."). Each group focuses on one calendar tradition. Groups note the month names, when the year begins, and which months hold the most important festivals.

Groups share findings in a quick round. Class builds a comparison chart on the board: calendar name | year-start month | one festival | moon phase used. Students add the new/full moon column by discussing what they know about the moon calendar and noting names like Purnima or Eid.

Closing discussion: what does it mean that different calendars can mark the same day as different dates? Students offer one observation each. Reinforce that measuring time is a human activity shaped by culture and astronomy.

periods.teacher_notes: Students bring genuine knowledge from home here — treat their responses as primary data, not anecdote. If the class is from a single community tradition, ask students to interview a parent or grandparent about one other calendar tradition; that knowledge can be shared at the opening of this unit. A common gap is that students may know festival names without knowing which calendar places them — guide groups to distinguish the calendar month name from the English month equivalent.
materials: Optional: printed or teacher-drawn month-name lists for Hindu, Islamic, or Sikh calendars

section_titles: How many hours in a day?
periods.activity_title: A Day in 24 Hours: Circle Diagrams and Digital Clocks

tasks_in_class.book_ref: How many hours in a day?, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Look at the doctor's 24-hour circle diagram. Write the number of hours spent on each activity and find the total number of hours from 6 o'clock morning to 6 o'clock morning the next day.
Fill in the blanks by writing time in the appropriate format — convert between AM/PM notation and 24-hour digital clock for given times.

time_bands.activity: Ask students: how many hours are in a full day? Take responses. Draw a large circle on the board and divide it roughly into a sleeping arc and a waking arc to build intuition before examining the textbook diagram.

Students open to How many hours in a day?, p.178 ("Look at the doctor's 24-hour circle diagram. Write the number of hours spent on each activity and find the total...."). Students read each sector, record the hours for each activity, and add them. The teacher circulates and checks whether the sum reaches 24; pairs resolve any discrepancy by re-reading the diagram.

Introduce AM and PM with the question: if a clock shows 8:00, is it morning or night? Briefly show the reference table on p.180 equating 12-hour and 24-hour notation. Explain the conversion rule (PM hours: add 12; AM hours: keep as-is, with midnight = 0:00).

Students work on Fill in the blanks, p.180 ("Fill in the blanks by writing time in the appropriate format...."). They convert a set of times in both directions — 12-hour to 24-hour and 24-hour to 12-hour. Two students share answers for class verification; highlight any systematic error in the PM-to-24-hour direction.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently write 12:00 PM as 0:00 rather than 12:00 in 24-hour format — the noon and midnight cases are the two exceptions to the add-12 rule and deserve explicit treatment. Connecting the 24-hour diagram to the doctor's daily life keeps the 24-hour total concrete before students handle the abstract notation. The circle-diagram total of 24 hours functions as a built-in verification: if a student's sector sum differs from 24, they know there is a reading error.
materials: Large circle drawn on board for opening

section_titles: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
periods.activity_title: Milk Trips and Homework: Adding Minutes to Clock Times

tasks_in_class.description: Raghav started homework at 10:20 AM and took 25 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face.
Muneera starts reading at 4:15 PM and finishes in 45 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face.
Akira leaves for school at 8:00 AM. Show times after +15 min, +15 min, +20 min, +10 min on the sequence of blank clock faces for school arrival, assembly end, dance practice end, break end.

time_bands.activity: Narrate Raghav's milk trip (8:20 to 8:35) from the chapter opening. Draw a blank clock face on the board, mark 8:20, and ask students how the minute hand moves when 15 minutes pass. Establish that the minute hand travels one full circle in 60 minutes — a reference point for the work ahead.

Students work on Let Us Do Q1a, p.181 ("Raghav started homework at 10:20 AM and took 25 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face....") and Let Us Do Q1b, p.181 ("Muneera starts reading at 4:15 PM and finishes in 45 minutes. Show the finish time...."). For each, students add the minutes and draw the resulting clock, then compare with a partner.

Students work through Let Us Do Q1c, p.182 ("Akira leaves for school at 8:00 AM. Show times after +15 min, +15 min, +20 min, +10 min on the sequence of blank clock faces...."). Students fill in each clock face in the sequence. The teacher pauses after the second clock to check the class is carrying forward the accumulated time correctly.

Brief share: one student draws the final clock from Q1c on the board. The class counts forward from 8:00 as a group to verify. Consolidate the key step: always count on from the current time, do not restart from zero.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is adding elapsed minutes to the hour number instead of the minute number — for example, writing 10:45 as 35 minutes instead of counting on from 20. Encourage students to say the minutes aloud as they count forward on the clock face before drawing. Q1c is a sequential chain; if a student has an error on the second clock, all subsequent clocks will be wrong — circulate early to catch this.
materials: Chalk/board with blank clock face drawn
Pencils for students to draw clock hands

section_titles: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
periods.activity_title: Half, Quarter and Three-Quarter Hours on the Clock

tasks_in_class.description: Observe four shaded clock diagrams. Fill in: half hour = ___ minutes; three quarters of an hour = ___ minutes. Deduce whether 1 hour equals 60 minutes.
Find out how much time you take to (a) boil milk and (b) fill water from tap in a bucket. What activities can you do in 5 minutes?
Three friends (Raghu, Raghav, Rani) read times from clock faces. Who is right? Discuss the error and explain how to read the clock correctly.

time_bands.activity: Display the four shaded clock diagrams from Observe the shaded portions, p.182 ("Observe four shaded clock diagrams. Fill in: half hour = ___ minutes; three quarters of an hour = ___ minutes...."). Students shade or count sector-by-sector, record 30 and 45, and state the deduction that 1 hour = 60 minutes. Pairs explain their reasoning to each other before the whole-class share.

Students engage with Find out, p.183 ("Find out how much time you take to boil milk, fill a bucket, and what you can do in 5 minutes...."). In the absence of real timing, students estimate in minutes and compare with neighbours. The class lists five-minute activities on the board; discuss whether five minutes feels long or short depending on the activity.

Present Let Us Check, p.183 ("Three friends — Raghu, Raghav, Rani — read times from clock faces. Who is right?...."). Students examine each friend's answer, identify the error, and write a one-sentence explanation of the mistake. Two or three students share their explanations aloud; the class votes on the best explanation and refines it.

Consolidating question to the class: if the minute hand points to 9, how many minutes past the hour is that? Students say the answer (45 minutes) and explain the counting-by-fives method. This anchors the clock-reading rule for the section.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often read the minute hand position as the numeral shown (e.g. minute hand on 9 → nine minutes) rather than counting by fives — the Let Us Check task is designed to surface exactly this error, so resist correcting it before students encounter it in the task. The shaded-sector diagrams are the concrete anchor for the half/quarter/three-quarter vocabulary; ensure every student has the textbook open at p.182 before the deduction step. The estimation activity in Find out is intentionally open-ended and should be kept brisk.

section_titles: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
periods.activity_title: Clock Relay: Consolidating Reading and Elapsed-Time Skills

tasks_in_class.description: Raghav started homework at 10:20 AM and took 25 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick oral warm-up: the teacher calls out a time (e.g. half past three, quarter to six) and students draw the clock face in the air or on a slate. This rehearses the half/quarter vocabulary from the hours-and-minutes section of the chapter before extended practice begins.

Students work independently on a relay of elapsed-time problems drawn from the hours-and-minutes section: starting with Let Us Do Q1a, p.181 ("Raghav started homework at 10:20 AM and took 25 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face....") as the entry task, then the teacher poses two additional oral problems (varied start times and durations, all within 60 minutes) for students to solve on the board or in their notebooks. The relay format means faster students pose a problem for a partner.

Pair-check: each student checks their partner's clock drawings by reading the hands aloud and comparing with the computed answer. Disagreements are resolved by counting forward from the start time together on a shared drawn clock on the board.

The teacher sets a brief exit reflection: name one situation from your own day where you would need to know when an activity will finish. Students say their answers; this connects elapsed-time reasoning to daily life and closes the section.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the elapsed-time and clock-reading skills built in the two preceding hours-and-minutes units — use the AM/PM and 24-hour notation from the AM/PM section when posing oral problems, so students practise identifying whether a time is morning or afternoon as well as drawing clock hands. If any students are still misreading the minute hand (numeral rather than count-by-fives), address this in the pair-check band; the Let Us Check task from the preceding unit having surfaced the error makes it easier to name. Additional practice: Let Us Do Q1b–Q1c (pp.181–182) may be used as consolidation or take-home.
materials: Slates or rough paper for oral round

periods.activity_title: Time All Together: A Chapter-Wide Synthesis

tasks_in_class.description: Notice the day on which July 15 falls; find August 15, September 15, October 15. What pattern do you notice? Challenge friends to guess the same date in the following month.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: How many hours in a day?, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Look at the doctor's 24-hour circle diagram. Write the number of hours spent on each activity and find the total number of hours from 6 o'clock morning to 6 o'clock morning the next day.
Fill in the blanks by writing time in the appropriate format — convert between AM/PM notation and 24-hour digital clock for given times.

time_bands.activity: Open the synthesis with a brief whole-class timeline on the board: the teacher draws a horizontal line from 'a minute' to 'a year', invites students to place the units — minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years — in order, and mark where the 24-hour clock, the calendar, AM/PM, and leap years each sit on that line.

Calendar strand review: students revisit Let Us Do Q9, p.177 ("Notice the day on which July 15 falls; find August 15, September 15, October 15. What pattern do you notice?...."). Students work in pairs to extend the pattern one month further and explain in writing why the pattern exists. Two pairs share explanations; connect the day-shift to the number of days in each month, bridging the leap-year and calendar content.

Hours strand review: students revisit How many hours in a day?, p.178 ("Look at the doctor's 24-hour circle diagram. Write the number of hours spent on each activity....") and then Fill in the blanks, p.180 ("Fill in the blanks by writing time in the appropriate format...."). Students quickly re-read two or three conversion entries they found difficult and self-correct before the partner-check.

Synthesis problem: the teacher poses an oral connecting problem — 'A doctor's afternoon clinic starts at 14:00. She works for 2 hours and 30 minutes. At what time (AM/PM) does she finish? Is the finish time before or after sunset?' — drawing on the 24-hour notation, elapsed-time addition, and AM/PM conversion all at once. Students solve individually, then compare with a partner.

Closing reflection: each student names one thing from the chapter they found surprising — the four-year leap pattern, the 24-hour total, a community calendar detail, or the count-by-fives minute rule. This surfaces the chapter's conceptual breadth and closes the synthesis on the students' own language.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the calendar content — leap years, elapsed months and years, day-shift patterns — the 24-hour circle, AM/PM-to-digital conversion, and clock-reading into a single connected picture. The connecting oral problem in the fourth band is intentionally multi-strand; students who find it difficult may be directed to break it into two smaller steps (convert to AM/PM first, then add the duration). The community calendars content explored in the Exploring other community calendars section is reflected in the closing reflection rather than a separate task, since that section's material is personal and variable.

items.prompt: Name one calendar used in India other than the English calendar. Write the name of the month in that calendar when an important festival in your community is celebrated.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any valid community calendar (e.g. Hindu/Vikram Samvat, Islamic/Hijri, Sikh/Nanakshahi). The month name should correspond to a real festival in that calendar (e.g. Kartik for Diwali, Ramadan for Eid, Vaisakh for Baisakhi). Accept any well-reasoned response grounded in a known calendar tradition.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the calendar explored and match its month to a known community festival.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student name just the festival and the teacher helps locate the month; stretch: name the corresponding English month as well.

exercise.description: Explore names of months in Hindu/Islamic/Sikh or community calendar. Find year-start, correspondence to English months, festival months, new/full moon patterns and their names.

items.section_title: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
items.prompt: Think of two activities from your daily life. Estimate how many minutes each activity takes. Write the activity name and your estimate.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two named daily activities with reasonable minute estimates (e.g. brushing teeth: 2–3 minutes; eating lunch: 15–20 minutes). Accept any estimate that is plausible for the activity described.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw on personal experience to estimate duration in minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: teacher suggests one activity and student estimates the other; stretch: student orders three activities from shortest to longest duration and explains.

exercise.description: Find out how much time you take to (a) boil milk and (b) fill water from tap in a bucket. What activities can you do in 5 minutes?

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: Which of the following years is a leap year?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2024. A leap year occurs every four years; 2024 is divisible by 4 and contains 29 February.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check which year is divisible by 4 to identify the leap year.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may not know the four-year rule and is guessing, or thinks any even year is a leap year.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may think leap years occur more frequently or that odd years can be leap years.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be off by one from the correct leap year, indicating an uncertain grip on the four-year sequence.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count by fours from 2024 on the board; stretch: ask the student to name the leap year before 2020.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks with consecutive leap years before and after 2024.

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: March 1 falls on a Sunday. On which day does March 8 fall? Explain how you found your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: March 8 falls on a Sunday. Eight days after March 1 is exactly one week and one day; one week later is again Sunday, so March 8 is a Sunday.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward in groups of seven days from the known Sunday to find the day for a date one week later.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write out the days of the week and count on a finger for each day; stretch: ask on which day March 15 falls.

exercise.description: July 1 is a Monday. Write the dates for the next two Mondays.

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: The 5th of a month falls on a Wednesday. The 5th of the following month falls on a Friday. How many days were in the first month? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first month had 30 days. Moving forward 30 days from Wednesday: 30 = 4 weeks and 2 days, so the day advances by 2, giving Friday. If the month had 31 days, the day would advance by 3 (to Saturday); if 28 days, by 0 (staying Wednesday). Only 30 days gives the Friday result.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the number of days in the month by 7 and find the remainder to determine how many days the weekday advances.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student try counting by 7s from Wednesday to see which number of days lands on Friday; stretch: ask what day the 5th falls on in the month after that.

exercise.description: Notice the day on which July 15 falls; find August 15, September 15, October 15. What pattern do you notice? Challenge friends to guess the same date in the following month.

items.section_title: How many hours in a day?
items.prompt: A student spent 8 hours sleeping, 6 hours at school, 3 hours playing, and some hours on other activities. How many hours were spent on other activities to complete a full day of 24 hours?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the known hours and subtract from 24 to find the remaining hours.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have added only two of the three given values before subtracting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have made an arithmetic error in the addition step, getting 15 instead of 17.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added the three known hours but did not subtract from 24, giving the sum rather than the remainder.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the circle with three sectors already filled and ask the student to shade the remaining sector; stretch: ask the student to write the four activities as a number sentence that totals 24.

exercise.book_ref: How many hours in a day?, p.178
exercise.description: Look at the doctor's 24-hour circle diagram. Write the number of hours spent on each activity and find the total number of hours from 6 o'clock morning to 6 o'clock morning the next day.

items.section_title: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
items.prompt: How many minutes are three-quarters of an hour?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 45 minutes. One hour = 60 minutes; three-quarters of 60 = 45.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Take three of the four equal quarter-hour portions of 60 minutes: 3 × 15 = 45.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is giving one-quarter of an hour rather than three-quarters.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is giving half an hour, confusing half and three-quarters.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is giving a full hour rather than three-quarters of it.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count four equal portions of the clock face and shade three; stretch: ask the student how many minutes are five-quarters of an hour.

exercise.description: Observe four shaded clock diagrams. Fill in: half hour = ___ minutes; three quarters of an hour = ___ minutes. Deduce whether 1 hour equals 60 minutes.

items.section_title: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
items.prompt: A clock shows the minute hand pointing to 9. A student says the time is 9 minutes past the hour. Is the student correct? Explain the mistake, if any, and write the correct number of minutes past the hour.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is incorrect. The minute hand on 9 means 45 minutes past the hour, not 9 minutes. Minutes are counted in groups of five for each numeral on the clock face: 9 × 5 = 45.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the numeral the minute hand points to by 5 to find the number of minutes past the hour.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count by fives starting from 1 on the clock face up to 9; stretch: ask what time is shown if the hour hand points to 3 and the minute hand points to 9.

exercise.description: Three friends (Raghu, Raghav, Rani) read times from clock faces. Who is right? Discuss the error and explain how to read the clock correctly.

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: Priya's birthday is on a Tuesday. What day is it two days before her birthday?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sunday. Two days before Tuesday: Tuesday → Monday → Sunday.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count backwards by one day at a time from Tuesday.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student counted forward two days instead of backward.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted back only one day instead of two.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted back three days instead of two.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write out the week in order and point to Tuesday, then move back one finger at a time; stretch: ask what day it will be three days after her birthday.

exercise.description: Answer questions by writing appropriate days of the week: today, yesterday, tomorrow, day after tomorrow, day before yesterday.

items.prompt: A train departs at 3:00 PM. What is this time in 24-hour digital clock format?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15:00. To convert a PM time to 24-hour format, add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 12 to the PM hour number to obtain the 24-hour equivalent.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not convert and simply wrote the 12-hour time, confusing AM and 24-hour notation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added 10 instead of 12, or confused 1 PM (13:00) with 3 PM.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 18 instead of 12, likely a computational error or confusion with a different PM hour.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student the reference table from p.180 and point to the 3 PM row; stretch: ask the student to convert 15:30 back to AM/PM format.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks by writing time in the appropriate format — convert between AM/PM notation and 24-hour digital clock for given times.

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: Renu was born on 10/03/2016. Her cousin Dev was born on 10/08/2018. How many years and months older is Renu than Dev?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Renu is 2 years and 5 months older than Dev. From March 2016 to March 2018 is 2 years; from March 2018 to August 2018 is 5 months.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the years from the earlier birth year to the later, then count the months between the same-date points in that final year.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student mark both dates on a drawn year-line and count the gap in steps; stretch: ask on what date Renu's 7th birthday falls.

exercise.description: Laali born 04/07/2014 and Chotu born 04/12/2019. Who is older and by how much? Find Laali's 5th birthday and Chotu's 10th birthday dates.

items.section_title: Leap years, months, dates and the calendar
items.prompt: A jar of jam was made on 05/09/2024. It is safe to eat for 6 months after the manufacturing date. On what date does it expire? Write the date in DD/MM/YYYY format.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 05/03/2025. Adding 6 months to September 2024: September + 6 months = March; the day stays 05 and the year moves to 2025.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the given number of months to the manufacturing month, carrying over to the next year if the total exceeds 12.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count forward on a printed month list (Jan=1 through Dec=12) starting from 9 (September); stretch: ask how many days remain if the student is reading this on 10/01/2025.

exercise.description: Check manufacturing and expiry dates on a biscuit packet wrapper. Find (a) how old the packet is and (b) how many more days it is safe to eat.

items.section_title: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
items.prompt: Arjun starts painting at 2:45 PM and finishes after 30 minutes. At what time does he finish? Write the time in HH:MM AM/PM format.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3:15 PM. 2:45 PM + 30 minutes: 45 + 30 = 75 minutes; 75 minutes = 1 hour and 15 minutes; 2:00 PM + 1 hour 15 minutes = 3:15 PM.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the elapsed minutes to the start minutes; if the sum exceeds 60, carry 1 hour and keep the remainder as the new minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a blank clock, mark 2:45, and count on the minute hand in steps of 5 to reach 30 more minutes; stretch: ask what time Arjun finishes if he paints for another 45 minutes after that.

exercise.description: Raghav started homework at 10:20 AM and took 25 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face.

items.section_title: Hours and minutes: reading clocks and elapsed time
items.prompt: Nadia starts her piano practice at 5:30 PM and practises for 45 minutes. At what time does she finish? Write the time in HH:MM AM/PM format.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6:15 PM. 5:30 PM + 45 minutes: 30 + 45 = 75 minutes = 1 hour and 15 minutes; 5:00 PM + 1 hour 15 minutes = 6:15 PM.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add elapsed minutes to start minutes; when the sum exceeds 60, carry 1 hour forward and write the remainder as the finish minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count 45 forward from 30 on a number line of minutes (0–60); stretch: ask how many minutes of practice Nadia completes between 5:30 PM and 7:00 PM if she takes a 15-minute break at 6:15 PM.

exercise.description: Muneera starts reading at 4:15 PM and finishes in 45 minutes. Show the finish time on the blank clock face.
